articles.text: The City of Piedmont will host a virtual discussion tomorrow, April 7, on equitable real estate practices that support an inclusive community. The event, entitled “Welcome to Piedmont: Real Estate Practices in Support of an Inclusive Community,” is co-sponsored by the Piedmont League of Women Voters, Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee, and Piedmont Racial Equity Committee. The discussion will be moderated by Piedmont resident Carol Galante, founder of the Terner Center for Housing Innovation at UC Berkeley. Panelists include retired Piedmont real estate agent Maureen Kennedy, a member of the Clinton Administration, Farrah Wilder, Chief Diversity and Equity Officer at California Association of Realtors, and Ashley Gardner, Community Outreach Coordinator for California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA). Residents and real estate professionals who tune in will learn about the current context for real estate practices and its impact on the demographics of the Piedmont community. A moderated discussion between the above professionals will focus on the benefits of an inclusive community and how Piedmont residents can help affirm the city’s commitment to be a more welcoming and diverse community. “Real estate transactions and the interplay between sellers, real estate professionals and potential buyers is one piece of a complex puzzle we are striving to solve... how to bring more diversity to Piedmont,” City Administrator Sara Lillevand said. “We look forward to an engaging dialogue focused on evolving practices and new ideas to help shape the Piedmont of the future.” In September 2021 Gov. Gavin Newsom signed into law over 30 affordable housing bills that focused on cutting red tape and holding cities accountable for providing their fair share of housing. To participate in this event, use the Zoom Registration Link at https://piedmont-ca-gov. zoom.us/webinar/register/WN_ zGnJ-AWnT4KFzrNxe2mKlg.

articles.text: Talk at Center for the Arts on Wednesday, April 20 Anastasia Edel on MSNBC Piedmont resident Anastasia Edel, author of Russia: Putin’s Playground, will speak at the Piedmont Center for the Arts at 7:30 p.m. on Wednesday, April 20 about Russia’s invasion of neighboring Ukraine, and its implications worldwide. Why did Vladimir Putin attack the sovereign nation of Ukraine, with which Russia shares centuries of common past? What’s behind the brutality of Putin’s war? How much popular support does he enjoy in Russia? Edel, an acclaimed writer, social historian and New York Times contributor, talks about her experience of growing up in the heavily Ukraine-influenced Russian south, the historical and cultural entwinement of the two countries’ natives, and the consequences of this war for Russia and the world. In lieu of an entrance fee, consider making a donation to Help Ukraine Center that supports refugees and distributes humanitarian aid. https://helpukraine. center/ A question and answer session will be held following her talk. Edel’s writing has appeared in The New York Review of Books, The New York Times, Foreign Policy, Project Syndicate, World Literature Today and others. She recently has appeared on CNN, PBS, NBC and MSNBC to discuss the crisis in Ukraine. articles.text: Piedmont teens and adults will be leaving for Mexico early Sunday morning, April 10 for five days on Piedmont Community Church’s annual Youth Service Trip to build homes near Tijuana during Spring Break. This year’s treasure sale raised $19,000 for building materials, travel costs and rations for the 205 volunteers who will build 12 houses for impoverished families. For more than 23 years Piedmont Community Church has sent a large group of volunteers south of the border to build homes. Scott Kail, Director of Student Ministries at the church took his first trip to Mexico 18 years ago when the crew consisted of 25-30 students and adults that built two homes. The annual trip – a rite of passage for many teens – was canceled in 2020 and 2021 due to COVID, making this year’s return extra special. The trip in 2019 was by far the largest in the event’s history with 320 volunteers building 20 houses. This year will be scaled back to 12 teams of 15 people each and will follow strict COVID protocols, requiring full vaccination, a negative COVID test Saturday April 9, and nearly constant mask wearing. On Sunday the crew will fly from Oakland to San Diego, where they will rent 15 passenger vans and a few pickup trucks. articles.text: Assembly Bill 1993, which would have mandated COVID vaccinations for all California businesses and independent contractors, was halted by its author, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks. Wicks, who represents Piedmont in the State Assembly, said she is putting the bill on pause to “allow space for conversations to continue and progress.” She introduced the bill to address concerns from employers and constituents who expressed the need for vaccine requirements in the workplace but felt unable to mandate it. “Our priority during this pandemic has been to make sure all Californians are as safe as possible by following the data and science around public health, which is why California continues to have some of the lowest COVID case rates, deaths and injuries per capita,” she said. Wicks added, though, that we are “in a new and welcome chapter in the pandemic, with the virus receding for the moment.” Her hope is to work more collaboratively with labor groups and employers to address concerns and questions raised by the bill. Strong opposition of the bill came from Wicks’ Republican colleagues, namely Assemblymember Kevin Kiley (R - Sacramento) who called the bill “radical.” “While I’m disappointed in the opposition to our bill by public safety unions, it’s my hope that they’ll ultimately come to the table to make sure all of their workers are vaccinated, and that every job sector in California has the tools necessary to keep their workers safe from COVID,” Wicks said. articles.text: Piedmont families are reading A Thousand Splendid Suns by Khaled Hosseini for this year’s community-wide Readmont project, now in its 12th year. articles.text: The following article appeared in the Post on March 10, 2021 when everyone was deep in COVID isolation. COVID has been the absolute worst for screen time and my kids. To say we have increased would be the understatement of the century. My boys use gaming as their only way of connecting with friends, so I say yes, because I know they are lonely and miss their friends. But if the boys are on their screens my daughter wants to be on...and the cycle continues. So, here are five totally wacky ideas to get kids off screens, even if it’s for just a few extra minutes. 1. Ipad Scavenger Hunt Hide the ipad. Yes, for real, hide it really well. Then create a series of clues directing your kids all over the house or backyard – or both – in order to find it. Clues can be simple, like “the place you might find a popsicle,” then they would go to the freezer and in the freezer find a note that says, “this is where you catch some ZZs,” so they go to their pillow on their bed, etc. etc. until they find their ipad. This doesn’t get them off screens for the whole day, but at least you know they spent a few minutes using their brains and moving their bodies first. 2. Make it a Game I am not necessarily advocating for a bribe in a traditional sense, but what if the next time getting you on! I don’t know about you, but I do not know how to play Roblox or Minecraft or Fortnite. Invite your kids to teach you how to play their favorite games. This becomes interactive and also a great way to connect and communicate while validating their interests and likes. 5. Live Action Video Game This one’s for when you’ve got a little bit of extra energy...which I understand is the hardest thing to come by right now as a parent. For little ones, can you encourage an imagination game that mimics their favorite video game? How do they “level up?” What are the obstacles they have to battle? Get the video off the screen and into their imagination. I hope these creative tools are helpful. In the meantime, let’s all be kind to ourselves. We have been parenting in the craziest time ever. Who needs mom-guilt on top of a pandemic? Maybe, they just play video games for an extra hour? I know I watched a ton of crappy 80s sitcoms in my childhood, and I came out OK...I guess. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department is seeking teenage volunteers for its “Summer Sidekicks” camp program. Teenaged “sidekicks” will be paired with campers in adaptive programing to help build relationships and strengthen children’s recreational skills. The Recreation Department is seeking teens age 14 or older who can commit to the summer session to be held on Thursday afternoons for six weeks. Community service hours and a letter of recommendation are available upon request. Teen sidekicks will attend a two-hour orientation and training program to learn about special needs and the basic principles. Each Sidekicks will be paired with a camper with special needs and should expect to meet with the camper and parent or family member prior to camp beginning. Teenagers who are interested should fill out the application at https://docs.google.com/forms/d/1BtA-6Ms7d26-bYp5u9AEDLlZ2t6q65IDrSeonT1Z8Q/viewform?edit_requested=true. The camp begins June 13. For more information contact Eva Phalen at (510) 604-3427 (ephalen@piedmont.ca.gov).

articles.text: Piedmont Scouts in Troop 11 spent the weekend of March 25-27 on an overnight camping trip to Pinnacles National Park near Soledad in San Benito County. Overall, the Scouts were excited about the trip, though they were tired after am epic 12-mile hike on Saturday. Their reward was a Patrol cook-off meal that night. The hike was very hilly with a lot of switchbacks. It went down and flattened out going through two talus caves known as the Balconies cave system. They ate lunch on a ridgeline in the cool shade of a large rock formation. From there they could see both the west and east entrance of the 26,000 acre park, known for its ancient volcanic formation. They went through a large cave, going under rocks that had fallen to create the Bear Gulch caves. They came out of the first cave near a small reservoir, where they took a small snack break. During the hike, the Scouts saw condors, turkey vultures, wild turkeys, deer, and plenty of ground squirrels. They hiked Scouts explore the talus caves. Troop 11 Scouts in the talus caves. articles.text: PHS tops San Lorenzo 22-12, Encinal 11-2 Piedmont’s softball team exploded last week with 33 runs in two games, defeating San Lorenzo 22-12 on Wednesday, March 30, and 11-2 over Encinal on Friday, April 1. Both games were at Witter Field. The dominant offensive display was highlighted by Morgan Hunt smacking a grand slam against San Lorenzo and a 3-run shot against the Jets. “I got a new bat,” said Hunt with a laugh. “I just have to believe I can do it and follow through. We’re the top team in the league right now, and if we can continue to hit this way, we’ll be able to make it far.” Staff Photos Senior Izzy Epstein hit her first career home run against Encinal. Gretchen Gerhardy had two RBIs and a run scored against San Lorenzo. Morgan Hunt was all smiles after hitting a three-run homer against Encinal. She also had a grand slam against San Lorenzo. Friday’s win also featured senior Izzy Epstein hitting the first home run of her high school career. She thinks wearing Chiara Lundin’s jersey due to a wash-machine mishap helped get the mojo going. “I was just shocked at first, and then I couldn’t stop smiling. It’s funny because I was wearing Chiara’s jersey, and she hits home runs all the time, and then I hit onel today,” said Epstein. The victories bring Piedmont’s record to 8-2 overall and 4-0 against WACC Shoreline Division teams. 11-2 over Encinal Piedmont scored once in the bottom of the second inning and twice in the bottom of the third. The Jets narrowed the deficit to 3-2 by the fifth inning, but PHS piled on six runs in the bottom of the fifth behind homers by Hunt and Epstein. They added two more runs in the sixth. Piedmont’s monster fifth inning was started by Angelina Wu’s leadoff slap single to center field. Leah Bell was hit by a pitch, putting two runners on base. With one out, Hunt smashed a shot to the left field fence. Lundin reached base on an error, setting up Epstein for her opposite-field home for two runs. In the bottom of the sixth, Lundin got an RBI double to score Miya Fujimoto, and Hunt scored on an error. Final stats: Hunt went 4-for-4 with a home run and a double, four RBIs and three runs scored. Epstein went 3-for-3 with a homer, two RBIs, and a run scored. Wu went 1-for-3 with two runs scored. Fujimoto went 1-for-3 with two runs scored and an RBI. Gretchen Gerhardy went 1-for-3 with an RBI and run scored. Epstein pitched a complete game with seven strikeouts and four hits allowed. 22-12 over San Lorenzo Piedmont led 8-1 after the first inning and 3-2 after the second, but it turned into an offensive barrage by both teams. San Lorenzo rallied to close the score to 15-12 by the fifth, but Piedmont had its own rally for seven runs in the bottom of the sixth, and won by the 10-run rule. Final stats: Hunt had a grand slam for 4 RBIs. Lundin went 3-for-3 with four runs scored. Gretchen Gerhardy went 1-for-3 with two RBIs and a run scored. Julia Banuelos went 1-for-2 with three runs scored and a walk. Bell went 1-for-3 with two runs scored and three RBIs. Wu went 2-for-2 with three runs scored, an RBI and walk. Epstein had a walk and two runs scored. Annabel Castronovo pitched four innings and Ginger Gardner entered in relief for the final two innings. Piedmont’s baseball team won two of three games last week, defeating league opponent Hayward 3-2 on Wednesday, March 30 at home, but losing to the same team 4-2 two days later on the road. The Highlanders followed up with a dominant 14-0 win at Oakland Tech on Saturday, April 2. Piedmont’s game-winning run March 30 came when Will Sprague stole home when Hayward tried to catch Markos Lagios stealing second base. Solid base running is a hallmark of an Eric Olson-led ball club. “We were just trying to grind one out. We had to get a guy on and get him over somehow and put some pressure on Hayward. We were able to get Will over to third; that was our ground-attack,” said Olson. Hayward’s team is the best in recent memory. Their pitchers did well with Kiefer Kiley and Nate Cordoba throwing complete games. “We saw at the beginning it would be a battle. They had a good pitcher. We came together in the last inning to grind it out,” said senior shortstop Nico Defazio. 3-2 win over Hayward The Highlanders took a quick 1-0 lead, but Hayward went ahead 2-1 by the in the top of the third inning. PHS tied it in the bottom of the fourth and didn’t score the winning run until the very end, in the bottom of the seventh inning. Pitcher Tobin Cantrill got the start and threw six innings with five strikeouts and six hits allowed. Sprague finished with a 1-2-3 top of the seventh. Piedmont’s opening run came with Lagios drawing a walk and stealing second. He advanced to third on a ground out, and with two outs, Davis Alazraqui smacked a hard ground ball through the infield to score Lagios. Down 2-1 entering the bottom of the fourth, Ryan McConathy drove in Logan Campbell from second with a single through the infield. Hayward tried to throw out Defazio at second base, resulting in Campbell making his way to home. With game tied 2-2 in the seventh inning, Sprague led off by drawing a walk. Lagios came through with a timely infield hit and beating the throw to first base. Sprague advanced to third on the botched throw. With Michael Aikawa at bat, Lagios stole second and the Farmers’ low skipped into centerfield. Sprague raced home for his second game-winning run this season. Final stats: Alazraqui went 2-for-3 with one RBI. Ryan McConathy went 1-for-3 with one RBI. Lagios went 1-for-3 with one run scored, stolen base, and walk. Defazio went 1-for-3. Sprague had a run scored and a walk. 4-2 loss to Hayward The Highlanders led 2-0 by the top of the fourth, but Hayward put up four runs in the bottom of the fourth and neither team produced any more scoring. Final stats: Aikawa went 2-forTobin Cantrill threw six innings with five strikeouts in Wednesday’s win over Hayward. Davis Alazraqui smacked a threerun homer against Oakland Tech.

Both games were at Witter Field. The dominant offensive display was highlighted by Morgan Hunt smacking a grand slam against San Lorenzo and a 3-run shot against the Jets. “I got a new bat,” said Hunt with a laugh. “I just have to believe I can do it and follow through. We’re the top team in the league right now, and if we can continue to hit this way, we’ll be able to make it far.” Highlanders shut out Tech, split games with Hayward Staff Photos Senior Izzy Epstein hit her first career home run against Encinal. Gretchen Gerhardy had two RBIs and a run scored against San Lorenzo. Morgan Hunt was all smiles after hitting a three-run homer against Encinal. She also had a grand slam against San Lorenzo. Friday’s win also featured senior Izzy Epstein hitting the first home run of her high school career. She thinks wearing Chiara Lundin’s jersey due to a wash-machine mishap helped get the mojo going. “I was just shocked at first, and then I couldn’t stop smiling. It’s funny because I was wearing Chiara’s jersey, and she hits home runs all the time, and then I hit onel today,” said Epstein. The victories bring Piedmont’s record to 8-2 overall and 4-0 against WACC Shoreline Division teams. 11-2 over Encinal Piedmont scored once in the bottom of the second inning and twice in the bottom of the third. The Jets narrowed the deficit to 3-2 by the fifth inning, but PHS piled on six runs in the bottom of the fifth behind homers by Hunt and Epstein. They added two more runs in the sixth. Piedmont’s monster fifth inning was started by Angelina Wu’s leadoff slap single to center field. Leah Bell was hit by a pitch, putting two runners on base. With one out, Hunt smashed a shot to the left field fence. Lundin reached base on an error, setting up Epstein for her opposite-field home for two runs. In the bottom of the sixth, Lundin got an RBI double to score Miya Fujimoto, and Hunt scored on an error. Final stats: Hunt went 4-for-4 with a home run and a double, four RBIs and three runs scored. Epstein went 3-for-3 with a homer, two RBIs, and a run scored. Wu went 1-for-3 with two runs scored. Fujimoto went 1-for-3 with two runs scored and an RBI. Gretchen Gerhardy went 1-for-3 with an RBI and run scored. Epstein pitched a complete game with seven strikeouts and four hits allowed. 22-12 over San Lorenzo Piedmont led 8-1 after the first inning and 3-2 after the second, but it turned into an offensive barrage by both teams. San Lorenzo rallied to close the score to 15-12 by the fifth, but Piedmont had its own rally for seven runs in the bottom of the sixth, and won by the 10-run rule. Final stats: Hunt had a grand slam for 4 RBIs. Lundin went 3-for-3 with four runs scored. Gretchen Gerhardy went 1-for-3 with two RBIs and a run scored. Julia Banuelos went 1-for-2 with three runs scored and a walk. Bell went 1-for-3 with two runs scored and three RBIs. Wu went 2-for-2 with three runs scored, an RBI and walk. Epstein had a walk and two runs scored. Annabel Castronovo pitched four innings and Ginger Gardner entered in relief for the final two innings. NEXT UP Piedmont (8-2 overall, 4-0 league) travels to Tennyson in Hayward tomorrow, Thursday, April 7 at 4:00 p.m. Staff Photos Will Sprague (center) celebrates with teammates Peter Krumins (left) and Nico Defazio. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s baseball team won two of three games last week, defeating league opponent Hayward 3-2 on Wednesday, March 30 at home, but losing to the same team 4-2 two days later on the road. The Highlanders followed up with a dominant 14-0 win at Oakland Tech on Saturday, April 2. Piedmont’s game-winning run March 30 came when Will Sprague stole home when Hayward tried to catch Markos Lagios stealing second base. Solid base running is a hallmark of an Eric Olson-led ball club. “We were just trying to grind one out. We had to get a guy on and get him over somehow and put some pressure on Hayward. We were able to get Will over to third; that was our ground-attack,” said Olson. Hayward’s team is the best in recent memory. Their pitchers did well with Kiefer Kiley and Nate Cordoba throwing complete games. “We saw at the beginning it would be a battle. They had a good pitcher. We came together in the last inning to grind it out,” said senior shortstop Nico Defazio. 3-2 win over Hayward The Highlanders took a quick 1-0 lead, but Hayward went ahead 2-1 by the in the top of the third inning. PHS tied it in the bottom of the fourth and didn’t score the winning run until the very end, in the bottom of the seventh inning. Pitcher Tobin Cantrill got the start and threw six innings with five strikeouts and six hits allowed. Sprague finished with a 1-2-3 top of the seventh. Piedmont’s opening run came with Lagios drawing a walk and stealing second. He advanced to third on a ground out, and with two outs, Davis Alazraqui smacked a hard ground ball through the infield to score Lagios. Down 2-1 entering the bottom of the fourth, Ryan McConathy drove in Logan Campbell from second with a single through the infield. Hayward tried to throw out Defazio at second base, resulting in Campbell making his way to home. With game tied 2-2 in the seventh inning, Sprague led off by drawing a walk. Lagios came through with a timely infield hit and beating the throw to first base. Sprague advanced to third on the botched throw. With Michael Aikawa at bat, Lagios stole second and the Farmers’ low skipped into centerfield. Sprague raced home for his second game-winning run this season. Final stats: Alazraqui went 2-for-3 with one RBI. Ryan McConathy went 1-for-3 with one RBI. Lagios went 1-for-3 with one run scored, stolen base, and walk. Defazio went 1-for-3. Sprague had a run scored and a walk. 4-2 loss to Hayward The Highlanders led 2-0 by the top of the fourth, but Hayward put up four runs in the bottom of the fourth and neither team produced any more scoring. articles.text: Parker Terrill awarded commemorative buckle for new school record in pole vault It’s not often a school gets to celebrate two new all-time records at the same time. On Saturday, April 2, Piedmont senior Jack Stein had an historic run at the Stanford Invitational, clocking a blazing time of 4:14.77 in the 1600 meters, edging past Tom Phelps’ record set 21 years ago by .15 of a second. In a furiously fast mole race at Stanford, Stein placed 8th in a field of 28 top runners from Photo by Jay Russell Piedmont’s new record holder, pole vaulter Parker Terrill, received an honorary belt buckle for his accomplishment. Northern California. “I didn’t come into the season thinking the mile would be in the book for me, I’m more of a 2-mile guy. I knew the race at Stanford was going to be a really fast race; I had raced some of the people in previous meets, and knew that I was only five seconds away, which was achievable but still difficult in the mile.” “It was so awesome – it was a huge-huge goal and accomplishment. I’m super proud of it,” said Stein. Piedmont’s all-time top-five times in the 1600 Jack Stein, 4:14.77 (2022) Tom Phelps, 4:14.92 (2001) Mark Ceraldi, 4:17.40 (2005) Will Sanford, 4:23.65 (2001) Reece Proctor, 4:24.70 (2017) Stein’s time was a 5-second improvement from his previous best, set March 19 at the Dublin Distance Fiesta. articles.text: The Highlander tennis team finished a successful week by beating league rival Berkeley 5-2 on Tuesday, March 29 at home but lost narrowly 4-3 to NCSfoe University on Wednesday, March 30 at Golden Gate Park in San Francisco. PHS then hosted Pleasant Valley from Chico on Saturday, April 2, and won easily 6-1. The University Red Devils won the Div. 2 North Coast Section in 2018 and 2019, so coach Jim Landes knew the match would be close. “If we had stopped this match just after halftime, we would have won handily. We were up 3 -1 with first doubles [Charlie Olcott and Kai Baudendistel] in the third set super breaker and Charlie Lambert and Lenni Burchardt in their second sets. But, we lost all three matches. It was a tough one, but we’ll get them next time,” said Jim Landes. The match at Golden Gate Park came with gusting winds and required major adjustments on the fly by Piedmont players. “The conditions at Golden Gate Park are very windy. Our opponents were very steady players and didn’t miss many shots or give us anything for free. The wind was definitely manageable, but took some getting used to,” said senior leader Kai Baudendistel. The batch of games brings Piedmont’s record to 10-2 overall, 7-0 in league, and puts them in the driver’s seat for the WACC title. They have four league matches remaining, starting tomorrow Thursday, April 7 with Alameda. The final matches come after Spring Break: Castro Valley on April 21, and O’Dowd on April 26. 5-2 over Berkeley Piedmont defeated the Yellowjackets by sweeping all three doubles matches and taking two of four in singles. In singles, Charlie Lambert lost 6-4, 6-4 at No. 1 against Leighton Sproul, and Lenni Burchardt lost a squeaker at No. 2, 7-6 (6-3), 6-4. Ben Breber won at No. 3 in straight sets, 6-3, 7-5, and Monte Imburg breezed to a 6-1, 6-2 victory at No. 4. In doubles, Charlie Olcott and Baudendistel won at No. 1 in straight sets, 6-2, 6-3; Ethan Pham and Brady Colbert paired to win No. 2 in three sets, 6-3, 2-6, 7-5; and Charlie Sullivan and Graham McWeeny easily won at No. 3, 6-0, 6-3. 4-3 loss to University University won the top three singles matches in straight sets and the No. 1 doubles match, barely beating Olcott and Baudendistel in doubles, 3-6, 6-1, 10-6. In singles, Lambert lost 6-2, 6-3 at No. 1 against Daniel Raviel. Burchardt at No. 2 lost 7-6 (6-4), 6-0, Breber at No. 3 singles, 6-1, 6-4, and Mr. Reliable, Imburg, came through with a 6-1, 6-2 win at No. 4. Pham and Colbert paired at No. 2 doubles won in straight sets, 6-2, 6-2, and Charlie Sullivan and Graham McWeeny rallied to win No. 3 doubles in three sets, 6-1, 3-6, 10-8. 6-1 win over Pleasant Valley Piedmont dominated the visiting team from Pleasant Valley, Staff Photos Kai Baudendistel played at No. 4 singles against Pleasant Valley and won at No. 1 doubles against Berkeley. winning three of four singles and all three doubles matches. Sullivan and Arun Brahma paired at No. 1 to win 6-3, 6-2; Carson Hicks and Jacob Hsia at No. 2 won easily, 6-1, 6-1; and the No. 3 pair of Nick King and Graham Alban opened the match with a 6-2, 6-0 win. Lambert lost No. 1 singles to Eugene Lee 6-2, 6-3; Breber won at No. 2 in straight sets; Pham at No. 3 won 6-2, 6-4l and in a rare singles appearance, Baudendistel won at No. 4, 6-4, 6-2. NEXT UP Piedmont (10-2 overall, 6-0 league) hosts Head Royce today, Wednesday, April 6 at 3:30 p.m. in a critical Div. 2 NCS matchup. They play again at Alameda High tomorrow, Thursday, April 7, also at 3:30. Ethan Pham won at No. 2 doubles against University and Berkeley, and also won at No. 3 singles against Pleasant Valley. Charlie Lambert is fully active after missing the first half of the season due to an injury.

articles.text: Shotgun Players is presenting a production of Passing Strange now through April 23. Directed by William Thomas Hodgson with music direction by Daniel Alley, the play follows the story of a young Bohemian who charts a course for “the real,” through sex, drugs and rock and roll. The play is set in Amsterdam, Berlin, and middle-class America. The show won a Tony Award for Best Book of a Musical. “Watching Passing Strange changed me and changed what my art could be. I just saw myself in this.” said director Hodgson. “There’s just something about the rock nature of this where I’m just having such a good time. The commune between the actors, the musicians, and the audience feels like centering in a theatre experience. There is something that’s so accessible in this play and in the writing.” The cast includes Angel Adedokun, Rolanda Bell, Myles Photo by Ben Krantz Devin Cunningham with Myles Brown (left), Angel Adedokun, Chanel Tilghman, and Shakur Tolliver in Shotgun Players’ current production of Passing Strange. Brown, Devin Cunningham, and Albert Hodge. For tickets, see https://shotgunplayers.org. Shotgun Players is located at 1901 Ashby Avenue in Berkeley. Tel.(510) 841-6500.

articles.text: Work of 40 artists to be displayed Piedmont’s 3rd annual Art Walk will take place in neighborhoods through the city on Saturday, May 7, and will feature 40 local artists representing a wide array of art. Under the leadership of founders Jon Schleuning and Larraine Seiden, the outdoor art exhibit will showcase paintings, ceramics, mixed media, sculpture, photography, jewelry, and textile art. articles.text: Jules Leyhe and The Family Jules Band brings some of the East Bay’s finest musicians to the Piedmont Center for the Arts for a show on Saturday, April 23. The band features saxophonist Nancy Wright, keyboardist Ian McArdle, and drummer Isaac Schwartz, who bring a funky jazz flavor to Leyhe’s fantastical vision. Leyhe’s eighth and most recent CD release, Your First Rodeo, has been featured in Premier Guitar and Vintage Guitar magazines. The band looks forward to playing an intimate East Bay show in Piedmont. A 2008 graduate of Piedmont High School and Berklee College of Music in Boston four years later, Leyhe’s career has included performances with legendary musicians Buddy Guy, Jimmie Vaughan, Huey Lewis, Chris Cain, Charlie Musselwhite, and Fantastic Negrito. Leyhe twice performed the National Anthem for the Oakland A’s at the Oakland Coliseum last year, and performs the Hendrix version of the National Anthem each year in the Piedmont 4th of July Parade. During COVID, Leyhe spent time as tour manager for blues legend Taj Mahal. The Family Jules Band stayed busy during COVID, recording three albums. Recent highlight performances include The Club Fox in Redwood City and Napa’s esteemed Blue Note. Tickets for the family-friendly concert in Piedmont are available online at https://bpt.me/5418175. Your First Rodeo CD This ain’t your granddaddy’s blues – heck it ain’t even your daddy’s blues. On this CD guitarist Jules Leyhe is on an entirely different trip, juxtaposing futuristic elements with down-home tones. He has been featured in Guitar Player, Premier Guitar, and Vintage Guitar. His album, Your First Rodeo, is a whimsical mashup of blues, hip-hop, fusion, rock and Latin music. Picture Duane Allman jamming with jazz piano great Gil Evans, or Jimi Hendrix playing in Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band. Jules Leyhe will perform at the Piemdont Center for the Arts on April 23.

Jazz improvisers began their development practicing such melodic designs but developed them into endless variations. Turnarounds became common in bebop through contemporary jazz music in the improvisations of Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie, Miles Davis, John Coltrane, Cannonball Adderley, Sonny Rollins, Stan Getz, Joe Pass, Barney Kessel, Wes Montgomery and George Benson. ter “Modal II-V-I Cadences and Turnarounds”. Turnarounds”/Building Turnarounds (link above). When a song is said to be in a key, a main note is the focal point of the piece of music. Sense of key can be defined in many ways, including the root of the chord you would expect the piece to end on. A chord “root” is the lowest imaginable note in a chord. You can play a “C” major chord with a “G” in the bass (one of its three notes), but if you imagine the lowest note played in the bass in a classic ending, the lowest imaginable note would be “C”. For common chords (triads, sevenths, ninths), organizing the notes of the chords in thirds (F-A-C-EG-B-D-F, etc.) would show the chord root as the lowest pitch. The common chord progression that establishes the I chord as a key (the “C” chord in the key of “C”) is V to I (“G” to C”). An elaboration of that idea evolved in classical music in creating a secondary progression to play the “V” of the “V” chord. In terms of the key of I (“C”), “V of V” is “II”. Dm-G-C is IIm-V-I in C. Progressive Late To Pickup Cadences (“Post Columns” link below) previews the harmonic use of II-V-I cadences while also showing top voice leading, cadence rhythms and comping rhythms. The eight examples progressively start II-V-I cadences earlier in the bar, showing they can be earlier at faster tempos. articles.text: “Every day, in every way, I’m getting better and better.” That’s the way people used to think in the not-too-distant past. I think that some French philosopher said it. These days it seems all that anybody says is, “misery likes company.” All the great musicians I have known were optimists. They were optimists even when faced with great adversity. Niccolo Paganini is a prime example. So is Beethoven. And how about the pianist Paul von Wittgenstein who resumed his career after his right arm was blown off during World War 1? I love the response of former heavyweight champion Floyd Patterson when reminded that he had been knocked down more times than any other champion, he replied, “But I got up more than any other champion.” He should have added, “and I won.” That’s why he was a champion. There are certain constants in music which are somewhat akin to an affirmative philosophy of life. Note that the opposite of negative is not positive – it is affirmative. Summer music camp, anyone? With summer fast approaching, perhaps you are thinking of sending the kids to a music camp. After studying countless books of music instruction, I have made a list of a few golden rules. Every one is phrased in the affirmative. 1) Have fun when you make music. 2) Always practice intelligently 3) Listen critically and ask yourself, “Do I really sound good, or am I deluding myself?” 4) Set goals for yourself. 5) Listen to the great performers of the past and pattern your interpretations after them. 6) Select good role models. From the genius we learn what to do. From the fool, we learn what not to do. 7) Develop secure techniques, including a seamless legato, a smooth por tamento, dynamics, tone production and rhythmic impulse. 8) Nuance. All of nature has nuance. Think of a blackand-white photograph. It has nuance. It is not “black or white“ with nothing in between. 9) Avoid pain. Listen to your body and know when to stop. Use the mirror and foster good body geometry. In order to sound good you must look good. Keep your body movements to a minimum. The more you move, the less control you have. 10) Use a metronome – it keeps you honest. 11) Always keep in mind that a secure technique allows you to “live dangerously on the stage.” 12) Consider every possibility, and then think for yourself. These golden rules have served musicians for a long time. Perhaps they have some bearing on today’s life.
articles.title: The antidote for negativity

articles.text: Entries due by April 15 Filoli House and Garden in Woodside is conducting a haiku contest based on its spring blooms. Interested participants may submit entries by April 15 and may submit up to three original haiku poems. The poems should be in the traditional haiku form of three short lines of five, seven, and five syllables. Submissions in languages other than English are strongly encouraged as long as they follow the haiku poem structure. Filoli is also launching the Filoli Ecopoetry Award this year, awarded to an individual whose haiku engages with the connection between humans and the environment. Haiku submissions should be inspired by Filoli’s spring garden and blooms. Judges will look for work that is eco-conscious and critical as well. Awards are as follows: First Place: Filoli Household Plus Membership and Gift Basket Second Place: Filoli Individual Plus Membership Best Under-18: Filoli Household Membership Filoli Ecopoetry Award: Filoli Household Membership A total of 10 semi-finalists will be announced on the Filoli website on Wednesday, April 22, and the four winning poems will be announced via social media on May 1. Visit https://filoli. org/haiku to submit original work.

articles.text: Matthias Schoenaerts stars in The Mustang. The Mustang is beautifully made, raw and unsparing, as well as being an example of fine writing. What might have been an obvious, shallow metaphor is instead a subtle and nuanced character study that resonates and compels. The story begins with a wide-angle shot of a large herd of wild horses roaming free on desert rangeland with a haze of blue mountains in the distance. Smash cut to these same horses being rounded up and herded by helicopter into large corrals. Some will be taken to Nevada’s Ely State Prison and become part of a Wild Horse Inmate Rehabilitation Program where prisoners are each given a horse to tame and then sold at auction to the Border Patrol, law enforcement, or private parties. That is the context. The narrative focuses on one inmate, Roman Coleman (Matthias Schoenaerts), doing 12 years for domestic violence. He has recently been released from solitary confinement and will again enter the prison’s general population, something he would rather avoid. “I’m not good with people,” he says. This opening scene shows Roman seated across from a staff psychologist-counselor (Connie Britton) who asks him a series of inane questions. Roman sits in silence, his laconic responses, when he makes them, barely audible, his emotional revetments impenetrable. Absent much discussion, she assigns Roman to an outdoor maintenance detail, cleaning stalls and corrals which means shoveling manure. This is his introduction to the horses and to the inmates who work with them. His attention is drawn to a ragged shed containing a wild mustang that is kicking and banging against the walls. Curious, he looks through an opening and then begins to open a narrow door, but is harshly admonished to stay away from the shed by the director-trainer for the wild horse program, Myles (Bruce Dern), who sends him back to his shovel and wheelbarrow. What is almost immediately evident is that the caged horse and Myles and the men who work with the horses have captured Roman’s attention. It’s not long before Myles senses the silent inmate’s interest. Pointing to the mustang now in a small corral, he explains that if he can spend just five seconds alone with the mustang, he is in the program. And thus begins what will be a difficult and painful journey for both Roman and this wild, dangerous, seemingly untamable animal that refuses to yield to its confinement. It’s evident that Roman faces not only the lethal rage of the mustang but his own. He is told by Myles that if he cannot control his anger (he confronts the mustang with his fists) he will be judged unfit for the program. He chooses to stay. This is a film of spare dialogue yet contains deep currents and a riptide of unexpressed emotions. What is revealed is a master class in acting, delivered by Schoenaerts. In one powerful scene, his estranged pregnant daughter, Martha (Gideon Adlon), barely out of her teens, comes to visit him for the first time in years. She wants only for him to sign a document allowing her to sell her grandmother’s house. He does, too quickly, and then tells her not to come back. But he fails to initial several pages and so she returns for a second and then a third time. With each visit, Roman’s wall of torment and alienation crumbles, a reality that is never conveyed by what he says but by the anguish etched in face, his attempt to look away into the distance failing him. And it’s in the final visit that Shoenaerts delivers what can only be described as a transcendent moment, the camera holding on his haunted eyes as he reveals to his daughter his remorse for the damage he has done to his family (and himself). Barely able to glance across the table, struggling for each word, he searches for a sign of redemptive forgiveness from Martha. But Roman finds his daughter protected by her own long ago constructed walls of judgment and memory. She simply stands and leaves. Roman’s journey is a given, but is not crafted from a series of clichés, nor does it find surcease in melodrama. Rather, it is created by writer/director Laure de Clermont-Tonnerre in such a direct and honest way that she finds the story’s metaphoric sweet spot and never backs away. If there is redemption to be found, it begins in the singular corral where that wild horse gives not an inch until it does. For Roman that makes all the difference. The Mustang is a wonderful movie. The Mustang. Directed by Laure de Clemont-Tonnere. Starring Matthias Schoenaerts, Gideon Adion, Bruce Dern, 1 hr., 36 min. Rated R. Now streaming on HBO Max/Prime. articles.text: David Sheff and his son Nic, the inspirations for the movie Beautiful Boy. Beautiful Boy is an adaptation of two memoirs, written by journalist David Sheff (Beautiful Boy) and his son Nic (Tweak). The titles for Sheff’s book and the film are lifted from John Lennon’s tender lullaby Beautiful Boy, composed for his son, Sean: “Have no fear, the monster’s gone/ He’s on the run and your daddy’s here.” It’s a haunting song and threads its way throughout the narrative, sometimes so softly it’s all but a whisper. And indeed, this film is about that ever-present promise that reassures: daddy’s here regardless of what life brings, so be not afraid. The monster is on the run. Only in Beautiful Boy the monster is crystal-meth (and other drugs) which grips David’s (Steve Carell) talented, gifted teenage boy, Nic (Timothée Chalamet), sending his life out of control, a spiraling descent into the jaws of addiction, He battles all who love him – his mother, Vicki (Amy Ryan); his stepmother, Karen (Maura Tierney); and his two small siblings who are impacted by the familly chaos that is felt but not understood. Nic’s journey into addiction is framed by a harsh and unforgiving anger and denial – remorse, reflexive dissembling, recrimination – as well as a sense of profound helplessness on the part of his father in Marin County and mother in L.A.. To describe Nic as he drifts away is to attempt to find an adequate metaphor. Perhaps it’s as if he is drowning, slipping under the waves, just within reach As he is momentarily pulled into the frantic embrace of his family, he slips from their grasp and so the cycle begins again: clean, sober, home, relapse, rehab. The anguish is palpable. The impotence is heartbreaking as Nic and his family confront a drug so powerful it actually alters the physiology of the brain. It is the monster. Early in the film there is a scene when David meets Nic at a small diner and they sit in a booth across from one another. David’s sense of desperation is evident, writ large in the grim set of his fearful eyes and his clenched jaw, wanting only to reach across the table and embrace his son with his words, to rescue Nic from demons that neither understands. It’s a harrowing scene, doomed before the first word is spoken, the ravages of Nic’s addiction there, before them. When he finally does get up, his stinging words suspended in the air, David is left to sit alone with his pain and isolation. He wonders what can he do? His beautiful boy. Throughout the film, director Felix Van Groeningen threads a series of fragile flashbacks of father and son together, each vignette conveying how deeply Nic is cared for. The cycle of addiction transforms those tender reflections into a dark dream in which Nic takes a wrecking ball to all of their lives. Truth is the casualty – spoken, shouted and ultimately framed by betrayal. Reason (you can do this, we can do this, rehab can do this) – becomes the unreliable scaffolding that is never enough. Beautiful Boy is a punishing story, difficult to watch, unrelenting in its unfolding, while also engaging and compelling. Over and over it reminds the viewer that addiction doesn’t just happen to the addict but to all who want only that beautiful boy back. The cast is superb, each portrayal convincing. The performances by Carell and Chalamet are remarkable, each a tour de force. Whenever David and Nic embrace and say goodbye, they whisper to each other one word, “Everything.” If only that word had the force and power to defeat the monster. Beautiful Boy. Directed by Felix vanGroeningen. Starring Steve Carell, Timothée Chalamet, Maura Tierney. 1 hr., 52 min. Rated R. Originally pubished in the Post in 2011.

articles.text: There’s a spoken line in the remarkable 2022 Oscar-nominated animated feature film The Mitchells vs. the Machines that is so quietly offered up, it will likely go unnoticed nu many viewers. Katie, the teen daughter of Rick and Linda Mitchell now away at college, in a zoom conversation with her parents, is asked the typical parental questions: “Are you getting enough to eat? How’s class?” But then Linda asks two unexpected questions, though not unexpected for the Mitchell family. Linda asks Katie, “Are you and Jade official?” Followed by, “Will you bring her home for Thanksgiving?” And with those questions, the film introduces a gay character (Katie wears a rainbow pin throughout). This zoom scene, which takes place during the denouement of the story, is included intentionally by co-directors Michael Rianda and Jeff Rowe. Rianda explained, “This is who she is. We wanted to say that this is a realistic family. We also did a lot of iterations to find the right balance. Ultimately, the story is about dealing with your family, and not about Katie’s sexuality. Her hair is red, she likes girls, and it’s normal. If it’s normal in real life, why isn’t it normal in animation?” We learn that before arriving at college Katie has been zooming with fellow students. One of them is Jade (Sasher Zamata), and it is made clear that the friendship has turned romantic once Katie arrived at the school. In thinking about this aspect of the film, it occurs to me that in all the animated films I’ve screened, I don’t recall ever even a nod being given toward a gay teen, or seeing a handicapped kid in a supporting role. Certainly there are countless handicapped youngsters who are enamored with animated feature films, and seeing a familiar face would be uplifting. Ditto Katie. Katie Mitchell, a gay character, in The Mitchells vs. The Machines.

articles.text: Hollywood writers have gotten a lot of mileage out of the dysfunctional family road trip, one that relies on a familiar trope: what can go wrong will go wrong. It usually results for the audience in headshaking chuckles to outright laughter. The Mitchells vs. The Machines is no exception. It was released in theaters and to Netflix streaming in April 2021, and received an Oscar nomination for Best Animated Feature Film at this year’s Academy Awards. At the center of this hilarious, emotive film is Katie Mitchell (Abbi Jacobson), a teen who loves movies, yearns to be a filmmaker, and dreams of moving to California, heartland of the fantasy industry. She lives with her mom, Linda (Maya Rudolph), a teacher and maker of grotesquely charming cupcakes; a pug named Monchi; her little brother Aaron (Mike Rianda), obsessed with dinosaurs; and her dad, Rick (Danny McBride), a hulking outdoors, Mr. fix-it guy with whom she doesn’t quite feel at ease. But then he’s the kind of guy who considers a non-slip screwdriver the perfect birthday gift, loves to build stuff, and worries that Katie’s dream of making movies will likely end in failure. So father and daughter are at an emotional impasse, and their relationship is often fraught with door-slamming tension and hurt feelings. Rick, confused, wonders where his little girl (who believed he could do anything) has gone, causing him to ask: who is this budding, newbie teen-stranger called Katie? Inspired, believing he has found a solution that will bring the family closer, Rick decides that what the family should do is not say goodbye to Katie at the airport as she heads off to college, but cancel her ticket and take a family road trip instead. Katie is not so sure, even a little mortified at the thought of arriving at her new college with (gasp) her parents. Nevertheless, so begins a series of really “wide-eyed”, “good grief ” misadventures from food poisoning to a visit to a seedy dinosaur theme park, all punctuated with minor family squabbles. Let’s just say that there is a lot going on, much of it hypermanic, filled with a variety of reactions that give new meaning to the term “bug-eyed.” Act three, unexpectedly, involves techie stuff, involving a hoodie-wearing IT guy named Mark Bowman (Eric André), a billionaire who has invented countless bots, and smart phones implanted with the ubiquitous voice of PAL (Olivia Colman). The bots are deemed benign and created to serve their master… oh, sure. As it turns out, the bots have a scheme to send all the humans into outer space and then create a bot-machine utopia. Naturally, it’s up to the Mitchells to save the world and undermine the bot plan and thereby avoid an impending apocalypse. The animation dazzles, the plot is a media-mix of cacophony and wonderfully stylized, audacious lunacy. But at the center of all the chaos is the Katie-Dad relationship in which they team up to save the world, and in the process affectionately realize the importance of the talents they each possess. Kids will be dazzled by the animation and the story. The Mitchells vs The Machines. Computer animation. Directed by Mike Rivanda and Jeff Rowe. With voices of Abbi Jacobson. Danny McBride, Maya Rudolph. 1 hr., 54 min. Rated PG. Now streaming on Netflix/Prime. Originally published in the Post in April 2021.

articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok A dish of Curry Codfish cakes is a nourishing and tempting meal. INSTRUCTIONS Easy enough for a weeknight dinner, these curry codfish cakes do not skimp on flavor nor appealing presentation. We have a version of codfish cakes on a nearly weekly basis. Curry flavors are near the top of the list of favorites, but I often change the flavor profile depending on what I’m craving; Spanish, Mexican, Thai, Chinese – well, you get the idea. Celery, shallots (or onion), diced tomatoes for moisture, and cilantro are staples in most versions. If you do not enjoy cilantro, flat-leaf parsley, mint or other herbs can be used as substitutes. Bonus Hint: Omit the raw egg and serve this delicious mix as a salad! I leave the crackers in larger pieces or toast up a piece of naan bread for extra crunch. Curry Codfish Cakes Makes 4 fish cakes INGREDIENTS • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • 1 pound codfish fillet, fresh or thawed 2 whole bay leaves 1 lime, divided into about 1/4 of it sliced to add to poaching liquid, the remaining lime juiced for adding to the codfish cake mixture 1 stalk celery, about 1/2 cup finely diced 1 medium shallot, about 1/2 cup finely diced 1/2 cup diced fresh tomatoes 1/2 cup fresh cilantro, coarsely chopped 1 generous tablespoon mayonnaise 1 tablespoon extra-virgin olive oil 2 teaspoons Dijon mustard 1 extra-large egg 3/4 cup coarsely crushed saltine crackers 1 tablespoon curry powder blend, to taste 1 teaspoon sea salt, to taste 5–6 whole black peppercorns, plus an additional 1/2 teaspoons freshly ground pepper, to taste Position an oven rack to the lower third position. Preheat the oven to 375°F, or on convection roast setting to 350°F. Line a baking sheet with parchment paper (optional but eases release of the fish cakes from the pan and clean-up). Poach the codfish: Place fillets, lime slice, bay leaves and a few black peppercorns into a 2-quart saucepan. Add water to just barely cover. Bring the water to a low simmer over medium heat, then continue cooking for about 6–7 minutes. Cooking time will vary depending on the thickness of the fish. Check as needed to ensure the fish just loses its transparency. Remove thinner pieces if needed. Important: Resist over-cooking. Drain and set aside to cool. If you fear you’ve overcooked the fish, cool it quickly with a bath of cold water. Combine the egg, mayonnaise, mustard, olive oil, lime juice, curry powder, sea salt and black pepper in a small bowl. Set aside. In a large bowl, mix the celery, shallot, tomatoes, cilantro, and cracker crumbs together. Flake the codfish fillets into the bowl, taking care to leave some of the pieces at least about onehalf inches in diameter. Gently mix the fish with the vegetables and crackers, then finally fold in the wet ingredients. Take care to preserve some large flakes of fish. Divide the fish cake mixture into four portions and shape into patties about 1-inch thick. Place on baking sheet and bake for 15-18 minutes until lightly browned and egg is fully cooked. If you use an instant-read thermometer, the middle of a fish cake should reach 160°F. Serve as-is, but a quick salsa of the same vegetables used in the fish cakes, with some minced jalapeno pepper or added cayenne pepper for a bit of zippy heat, is a nice upgrade.

articles.text: A kind, generous, and compassionate man with a hilarious and fun sense of humor, Jeff Retherford left us too soon. Jeff passed away peacefully at home surrounded by his loving family on December 14, 2021 following a 3-month battle with Pancreatic cancer. Jeff meant so much to so many. With his easy nature and “gift of gab,” he easily made friends wherever he went, including making several friends within weeks of joining exercise and yoga classes at the Berkeley Ironworks climbing gym. Whether discussing World history, current events, or helping young adults write résumés and figure out their path in life, his ability to put others at ease and make them laugh drew others to him and earned him the status of “favorite Uncle Jeff.” In his role as Director of Cardiac Services at Summit Hospital, Jeff leaves behind the legacy of bringing the STEMI and TAVR cardiac programs to several Bay Area hospitals. Many people are alive today because of his direct intervention. Beginning as a glider pilot while still a teenager, one of Jeff’s passions was flying his Cirrus SR22. The familiar phrase of “wheels up” meant the start of another fun adventure, even if it was just ferrying his kids to college. Always willing to lend a hand and share his skills as a “Jack-ofall-trades,” Jeff will be remembered fondly by the many teams of students he mentored as a volunteer leader with Piedmont Community Church’s Mexico house-building mission trips Jeff Retherford passed away on December after a 3-month battle with cancer. during Spring Break. He was the Dad who worked hard, insisting on construction precision, but who also loved a good prank. Jeff appreciated the beauty in nature and enjoyed hiking with his family; his presence just made everything more fun, including his “bad Dad jokes,” silliness, and pranks thrown in at unexpected moments to keep us on our toes. He loved learning new things and was becoming quite the apiarist, leaving behind 2 active hives that his neighbors are graciously stepping in to help manage. Jeff will be missed tremendously by all who knew him. His absence is palpable by his neighbors on Carmel Avenue, whom he was honored to call his friends. Jeff was most proud of his wife, two sons and daughter and their accomplishments, and really wanted to stick around to be a part of their lives as they unfolded. The feeling is mutual: we miss you, honey.

articles.text: A large group was on hand March 30 for the weekly Walking on Wednesdays excursion. Pictured are: Priscilla Wanerus, Lynn Richmond, Jo Normington with K-9 best friend Penny Lane, Alicia Rivera, Charlene Louie, Dena Belinkoff, Ken Young, Kat Lang, Judy Wang, Harriette Louie, Alan Goldhammer, Tyler Johnson, Jim Kuo, Marion Lim Yankowitz, SiowFang Tan, Mike Henn, Pat McMahon, Martin Levy, Brenda Ferrero, Pat Sheehan, Pat Keller, Sherry Jacobs, Edith Lee, Lilly Guardia-Labar, Albert Chen, Renee Goldhammer, and Dick Carter. On a cool Wednesday morning, March 30, 28 walkers and one K-9 best friend were at the Exedra for the weekly Walking on Wednesdays stroll through the city. The group wanted to complete some unfinished business. In February the Post had reported on two Public Works projects, retaining walls on San Carlos and Oakland Avenue. The destination this day was Oakland Avenue at Sunnyside Avenue, which the group had not seen since its retaining wall was completed. The walk took the group across the Oakland Avenue Bridge and on Sunnyside, Lake, Linda, and Rose Avenues to see the northwest side of Piedmont. Based upon information from Gail Lombardi, president of the Piedmont Historical Society, Oakland Avenue Bridge was the historic entrance to Piedmont. Albert Farr designed it in 1910 as a significant entrance to Piedmont. Farr used the same Spanish design that he had used in the Piedmont City Hall and the Bonita Avenue School (later named Havens School). The bridge replaced an old wood trestle that was built in 1890 for the cable cars that served the area in its early years. The bridge was designed in 1911 by John Buck Leonard of Union City, Michigan, who was a pioneering bridge designer, architect, and early advocate for reinforced concrete structures. It is a concrete arch bridge over Linda Avenue with a 160-foot arch span and retaining wall supported approaches in a closed spandrel concrete deck arch design. The largest span is 159 feet and the total length is 343 feet, which is more than a football field. The new lampposts, lights, and guardrails make the Oakland Avenue Bridge a lovely entrance to the city. At the high end of the bridge is the new retaining wall. The walkers continued up Sunnyside to Lake Avenue, then onto Linda Avenue past Beach School. One block later they came to the lovely fully landscaped Linda-Kingston Triangle built in 2016 as a project paid by the city and neighborhood residents. A handsome stone bench was built into the wall facing out to Linda Avenue at the 3-way corner of Linda, Kingston and Rose Avenue, one of the city’s boundary with the city of Oakland. The group crossed Linda and went a short distance up it to Rose Avenue. It was reported that this is one of the oldest streets in Piedmont. Actually, only the south side of the street is in Piedmont. The Oakland/Piedmont city line runs through the middle of it, and its north side homes are in Oakland. The walkers noted a beautiful, restored, gray with white trim “Cottages & Castles” Victorian built in 1894. A set of stairs leads up to its front door and there are a turret and two gables as part of its roof. The walkers crossed Grand Avenue and went down (and up) Arroyo Avenue to Monticello Avenue. They noted a hidden pathway that goes to the Lorita Avenue cul-de-sac, which they had missed on a previous walk. The group turned onto Ramona Avenue and made their way to the well named Bonita Avenue (pretty in Spanish). A right on Bonita brought the group back to Magnolia Avenue, where they passed lovely cedar shake shingle homes, draught tolerant gardens, pink dogwoods, emerging red bud blossoms, primroses, and other front yard beauty; as well as Havens School playground enthusiasts. The walkers emerged on Magnolia, one block from their starting point. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome nu registering with the Piedmont Recreation Department at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. FUTURE WALKS On April 20 and 27 Hope Salzer will take the walkers on sneak preview tours of two Piedmont gardens that will be part of the 18th Annual “Bringing Back the Natives Garden Tour and Green Home Features Showcase.” After that former Piedmont Mayor Bob McBain will host the walkers on a visit to Tyson Lake at the back of his Sotelo Avenue home. By Dick Carter On a cool Wednesday morning, March 30, 28 walkers and one K-9 best friend were at the Exedra for the weekly Walking on Wednesdays stroll through the city. The group wanted to complete some unfinished business. In February the Post had reported on two Public Works projects, retaining walls on San Carlos and Oakland Avenue. The destination this day was Oakland Avenue at Sunnyside Avenue, which the group had not seen since its retaining wall was completed. The walk took the group across the Oakland Avenue Bridge and on Sunnyside, Lake, Linda, and Rose Avenues to see the northwest side of Piedmont. Based upon information from Gail Lombardi, president of the Piedmont Historical Society, Oakland Avenue Bridge was the historic entrance to Piedmont. Albert Farr designed it in 1910 as a significant entrance to Piedmont. Farr used the same Spanish design that he had used in the Piedmont City Hall and the Bonita Avenue School (later named Havens School). The bridge replaced an old wood trestle that was built in 1890 for the cable cars that served the area in its early years. The bridge was designed in 1911 by John Buck Leonard of Union City, Michigan, who was a pioneering bridge designer, architect, and early advocate for reinforced concrete structures. It is a concrete arch bridge over Linda Avenue with a 160-foot arch span and retaining wall supported approaches in a closed spandrel concrete deck arch design. The largest span is 159 feet and the total length is 343 feet, which is more than a football field. The new lampposts, lights, and guardrails make the Oakland Avenue Bridge a lovely entrance to the city. At the high end of the bridge is the new retaining wall. The walkers continued up Sunnyside to Lake Avenue, then onto Linda Avenue past Beach School. One block later they came to the lovely fully landscaped Linda-Kingston Triangle built in 2016 as a project paid by the city and neighborhood residents. A handsome stone bench was built into the wall facing out to Linda Avenue at the 3-way corner of Linda, Kingston and Rose Avenue, one of the city’s boundary with the city of Oakland. The group crossed Linda and went a short distance up it to Rose Avenue. It was reported that this is one of the oldest streets in Piedmont. Actually, only the south side of the street is in Piedmont. The Oakland/Piedmont city line runs through the middle of it, and its north side homes are in Oakland. The walkers noted a beautiful, restored, gray with white trim “Cottages & Castles” Victorian built in 1894. A set of stairs leads up to its front door and there are a turret and two gables as part of its roof. The walkers crossed Grand Avenue and went down (and up) Arroyo Avenue to Monticello Avenue. They noted a hidden pathway that goes to the Lorita Avenue cul-de-sac, which they had missed on a previous walk. The group turned onto Ramona Avenue and made their way to the well named Bonita Avenue (pretty in Spanish). A right on Bonita brought the group back to Magnolia Avenue, where they passed lovely cedar shake shingle homes, draught tolerant gardens, pink dogwoods, emerging red bud blossoms, primroses, and other front yard beauty; as well as Havens School playground enthusiasts. The walkers emerged on Magnolia, one block from their starting point. In that evil is undoubtedly alive and well, often seeming to driven by its own life force, I find the perspective of Enoch to be worthy of serious consideration. Equal in importance to Enoch’s understanding of evil is its articulation of hope. In its apocalyptic worldview, hope is outside human striving. It is not created by human intention. It is solely the will and work of God. Expressive of this hope are the four archangels Enoch identifies: Michael, Raphael, Gabriel and Phanuel. Michael is “merciful and long-suffering.” Raphael is “set over all the diseases and all the wounds of the children of men.” Gabriel is “set over all the powers.” Phanuel is “set over the repentance unto hope of those who inherit eternal life.” In Enoch’s vision, evil is alive and well. Yet, so is divine hope. Divine hope is not dependent on our efforts. It comes from God alone. It comes on the wings of angels who have power over those forces that hurt and harm. for aging.
